Welcome to Lecture 2 of the CS217: AI-ML Course by IIT Bombay, delivered by Prof. Pushpak Bhattacharya.

In this lecture, we continue exploring the concept of Search in Artificial Intelligence. The session covers various search problems and their significance in AI, including practical examples like:

🔎 Topics Covered:

Search as a core concept in AI and its applications in various fields.
Block World Problem: Understanding search through the example of arranging blocks in a goal configuration.

Correspondence Problem in Computer Vision: How depth perception works using two retinal images and matching points.

Robotic Path Planning: Solving navigation problems for robots by avoiding obstacles and choosing optimal paths.

Expert Systems and Rule-Based Search: Exploring how search is applied in medical diagnosis and decision-making through expert systems.

State Space and Operators: Introduction to formalizing search problems using state-space graphs, operators, and cost functions.

8-Puzzle Problem: An example of search where tiles need to be rearranged to reach a goal state using minimum moves.

Missionaries and Cannibals Problem: A classical search problem that highlights state description, constraints, and the role of operators.

Search in Natural Language Processing (NLP): Parsing complex sentences, like the famous "Buffalo" sentence, through search techniques.

Designing Efficient Search States and Operators: Importance of relevant attributes and cost functions in search optimization.

title: My AI/ML track in IIT Bombay - Jimut Bahan Pal
description: Inspired from this and this post, I am sharing my views and materials that were generated by taking some of the courses, here at IIT Bombay, for my future reference. To be honest there are no such AI/ML tracks here at IIT Bombay, but one can make according to their requirements. I am enrolled here as a PhD in C-MInDS department, and for some obvious obligatory reasons, I need to do an AI/ML track which was curated by my supervisor, since he is the best in recommending courses. This is from the IEOR department, and one of my favorite courses taught by P. There are no such requirements for this course, except one needs to be comfortable with Python3 and should have some knowledge of machine learning and Pytorch. So, if you are really into Deep Learning and need to take a course, I will surely recommend this one.
